newsitem.title: FRANCE: Le Pen boosted by French poll, hits out at Chirac.
newsitem.headline: Le Pen boosted by French poll, hits out at Chirac.

text.p: Far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, buoyed by a likely local election victory, said on Sunday he planned to make his party France's biggest and weighed in against President Jacques Chirac and his party.

Le Pen, whose anti-immigration party according to early estimates won a fourth southern French town in Vitrolles in a municipal elections, acknowledged that Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe had ruled out any accord with his party.
"So between them and us, it's a struggle to the finish because it's not certain that Juppe and Chirac will always be leading France," Le Pen told Europe-1 radio in an interview.
He said France would have fared better if Socialist leader Lionel Jospin had defeated Chirac in presidential elections.

"Given the demagogy of Chirac's campaign and knowing the prejudices he had towards the values of the (Front) especially, knowing also the high level of corruption of French political circles and especially of the party presided by Mr Chirac and perhaps of Chirac himself..." Le Pen said before interviewers interrupted him.

"It wasn't Mr (Jean) Tiberi who was mayor of Paris," Le Pen added in a reference to political corruption probes focusing on the capital's administration at a time when Chirac was mayor, and the Gaullist RPR party previously led by Chirac.

Le Pen claimed victory within minutes of polls closing in the Vitrolles -- a contest watched by the whole of France -- and said that it demonstrated his party -- currently at around 15 percent nationally -- was capable of becoming the country's biggest.

The first estimates, based on the first 1,900 out of a total 16,400 ballots, showed Front candidate Catherine Megret, wife of the party's number two Bruno Megret, won 52.35 percent of the vote, against Socialist Jean-Jacques Anglade's 47.65 percent.
"Who can say that the National Front is not capable of becoming France's first party? If you judge from the Vitrolles microcosm, you realise that it's possible," Le Pen said.
Le Pen added that the French would come to realise "the shortcomings of those who lead them and...the failure to resolve major problems like unemployment, immigration, and taxes."
